title: Juice it or lose it - a talk by Martin Jonasson & Petri Purho
summary: Two indie developers start from a flat grey Breakout clone and switch on one small effect at a time: colour, tweened entrances, squash and stretch, sound, particles, screen shake and finally eyes on the paddle. The point is that 'juice' is cascading, exaggerated feedback to minimal input, and that stacking many cheap effects turns a dead form-like screen into something that feels alive.

insights.insight: Juice is a catch-all for responses that wobble, bounce, squirt or make little noises: the game answers every small input with a cascade of reaction. A screen that only changes state silently reads as software, not as a game.
insights.quote: a juicy game feels alive in response to everything you do
insights.visual: The slide behind the speakers is a grid of easing curves, the toolkit they use to make every change move with character instead of snapping.

insights.insight: The baseline is a correct, fully playable game made of plain white rectangles on grey. It works but feels lifeless, exactly like a functional UI form: correctness is not what makes something feel like a game.
insights.visual: The un-juiced Breakout: a block grid of identical white bars and a flat paddle, no colour, no motion, no personality.

insights.insight: Nothing should teleport. Even without a tweening library, moving a value a fixed fraction toward its target each frame gives a fast-then-settling motion. Then entrances get easing with overshoot, elastic bounce, rotation, scale and a small random delay per item so a grid assembles itself instead of appearing.
insights.visual: The one-line easing formula on screen, the cheapest way to give any position, size or opacity change a natural ease-out.

insights.insight: Sound is the most cost-effective juice and the most neglected. The same animation of two circles reads as passing through each other when silent, and as colliding and bouncing once a hit sound plays on the exact frame of contact.
insights.visual: The Steve Swink two-circles demo: identical motion shown twice, with and without a collision sound, to prove sound changes perceived physics.

insights.insight: Screen shake on impact makes the ball feel heavy and powerful for almost no effort, and a trail drawn from recent positions makes speed visible. Both are strong spices: dose them to the importance of the event.
insights.visual: Mid-rally with a long yellow ball trail streaking across the screen while the camera shakes on each hit.

insights.insight: Giving an object eyes that blink, follow the ball, and a mouth that smiles on success or frowns when the ball gets away adds huge personality for tiny cost: the UI element becomes a character that reacts emotionally to what the player does.
insights.visual: The paddle now wears big cartoon eyes looking toward the ball, the cheap character trick (added at 13:03) that turns a bar into a companion.

insights.insight: No single effect is impressive; the transformation comes from stacking dozens of small ones until every action triggers colour, motion, particles, sound and a reaction. Before/after comparison is the best test.
insights.visual: The final all-effects-on state: ball trails, confetti and particles fill the screen and the eyed paddle reacts, contrasted with the grey baseline at 02:15.

apply_to_wael: Never let a choice screen appear statically: level and subject choices should assemble into the scene with eased, staggered entrances (slight overshoot, 40-80 ms random delay per item) and leave with a tween, so pick-level -> pick-subject feels like the camera moving, not a page swap.

Every tap on a choice gets a full juice stack on the same frame: squash on press, stretch/bounce on release, a short sound, a small particle puff in brand colours, and a reaction from Wael. A correct answer in the 3-question game earns stronger juice (bigger burst, light screen shake, Wael cheering) than a neutral selection.

Treat Wael as the 'eyes on the paddle': instead of sitting boxed in a side panel, he should live in the scene and react to the player's input (look at the hovered/pressed option, nod, smile on a correct answer, wince on a wrong one).

Run the before/after test from the talk on the current flow: record the welcome -> result screens with juice off and on; any screen that still looks like the grey baseline (white cards in a grid, static progress bar) needs colour, motion and sound added before it can sit next to the 3D splash.
